Let $g_t = p_t(E)$.
Using Equation~\eqref{eq:derivative_pt}, we obtain the following derivative of $g_t$
\begin{align*}
  d g_t &= \int_E (x - \mu_t)^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t p_t(x) dx.
\end{align*}
Its quadratic variation is
\begin{align*}
  d\brackets{g}_t &= \vecnorm{\int_E A^{-1/2} (x - \mu_t) p_t(x) dx }{2}^2 dt \\
  &= \max_{\vecnorm{\xi}{2} \leq 1} \parenth{\int_E \xi^\top A^{-1/2} (x - \mu_t) p_t(x) dx}^2 dt \\
  &\leq \max_{\vecnorm{\xi}{2} \leq 1} \parenth{\int_E \parenth{\xi^\top A^{-1/2} (x - \mu_t)}^2 p_t(x) dx} \parenth{\int_E p_t(x) dx} dt \\
  &\leq \max_{\vecnorm{\xi}{2} \leq 1} \xi^\top A^{-1/2} A_t A^{-1/2} \xi dt \\
  &= \vecnorm{A^{-1/2} A_t A^{-1/2}}{2} dt,
\end{align*}
where the inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
Applying the Dambis, Dubins-Schwarz theorem (see e.g. Revuz and Yor~\cite{revuz2013continuous} Section V.1 Theorem 1.7), there exists a Wiener process $\tilde{W}_t$ such that $g_t - g_0$ has the same distribution as $\tilde{W}_{[g]_t}$. Since $g_0 = \frac{1}{2}$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
  \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\parenth{\frac{1}{4} \leq p_t(E) \leq \frac{3}{4}} &= \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\parenth{-\frac{1}{4} \leq \tilde{W}_{[g]_t} \leq \frac{1}{4}} \\
  &\geq 1 - \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\parenth{\max_{0 \leq s \leq \frac{1}{64}} \abss{\tilde{W}_s} > \frac{1}{4}} - \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}([g]_t > \frac{1}{64}) \\
  &= 1 - 4 \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\parenth{\tilde{W}_{\frac{1}{64}} > \frac{1}{4}} - \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\parenth{[g]_t > \frac{1}{64}} \\
  &\geq \frac{9}{10} - \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\parenth{\int_0^t \vecnorm{A^{-1/2} A_t A^{-1/2}}{2} ds > \frac{1}{64}},
\end{align*}
where the last inequality follows from the fact that $\ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}\parenth{\xi > 2} < 0.023$ for $\xi$ follows the standard Gaussian distribution.

Then through a change of variable, we have
\begin{align*}
  &\mathcal{T}_p \parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} \\
  =& \int\int (x-\mu)^\top A^{q-2} (y-\mu) \cdot (x-\mu)^\top (y-\mu) \cdot (x-\mu) ^\top (y-\mu) p(x) p(y) dx dy \\
  =& \int\int \parenth{x^\top A^{q-1} y} (x^\top A y) (x ^\top A y) \varrho(x) \varrho(y) dx dy \\
  \leq& \int\int \parenth{x^\top A^{q} y} (x^\top A y) (x ^\top y) \varrho(x) \varrho(y) dx dy \\
  =& \mathcal{T}_\varrho \parenth{A^{q}, A, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}},
\end{align*}
where the last inequality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ttensor_swap}. $A^q$ is positive semi-definite and we write down its eigenvalue decomposition $A^q =  \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i v_i v_i ^\top$ with $\lambda_i \geq 0$. Since $\varrho$ is isotropic, we can rewrite the 3-Tensor into a summation form and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound}.
\begin{align*}
  &\mathcal{T}_\varrho \parenth{A^{q}, A, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} \\
  & = \int \int \parenth{x ^\top A^q y} \parenth{x ^\top A y} \parenth{x^\top y} \varrho(x) \varrho(y) dx dy  \\
  & = \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i \int \int \parenth{x ^\top v_i} \parenth{y ^\top v_i} \parenth{x ^\top A y} \parenth{x^\top y} \varrho(x) \varrho(y) dx dy  \\
  & = \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i A \Delta_i} \\
  &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq}  128 \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}(A^{1/2\beta})}^{2\beta} \parenth{\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i} \\
  &= 128 \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}(A^{1/2\beta})}^{2\beta} \mathrm{Tr}(A^q) \\
  &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} 128 \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \mathrm{Tr}(A^q) \brackets{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}^{1/(2\beta q)} \parenth{\ensuremath{d}}^{1 - 1/(2\beta q)}}^{2\beta} \\
  &= 128 \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \ensuremath{d}^{2\beta - 1/q} \mathrm{Tr}(A^q) ^{1 + 1/q},
\end{align*}
where we define $\Delta_i = \int (x^\top v_i) x x^\top \varrho(x) dx$, inequality (i) follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound} and that $\varrho$ is isotropic, inequality (ii) follows from Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the assumption that $q \geq \frac{1}{2\beta}$.
